prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength reach a fractional uncertainty near 10^-18 and open millimetre-scale tests of gravitational redshift and of the constancy of fundamental constants

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my single-part choice, and the first round has sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The chair asks what is new compared with 2005 and 2012. My answer is the magic-wavelength lattice itself. Katori's proposal is to choose the trap wavelength so that the light shift is equal for the two clock states, which lets many thousands of neutral atoms be held without Doppler or recoil shifts and interrogated in parallel. The 2005 prize honoured the comb, which is the ruler that counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize honoured the control of a single quantum system. Neither contains the idea that a large ensemble can be made insensitive to the trap that holds it. That idea changes the counting statistics, so stability at the 1e-18 level becomes reachable in hours and not weeks, and that in turn is what made new measurements possible: the gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres inside one atomic sample, comparisons between laboratories at the 1e-18 level, and bounds on drifts of constants. Ye's group carried the concept to that performance and showed what the stability and systematic control allow. The result is robust in the sense I value: JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE have built and compared lattice clocks, and the systematic shifts (blackbody radiation, higher-order lattice terms, collisions) are calculated, measured and then checked against each other. My own field supplies much of that theory, so I can say that the agreement is not cosmetic. Having read the round-1 statements, I notice that the case against B009 offered by its own supporters, the open pairing mechanism and the attribution questions, is a case I cannot fully answer with the confidence I have for the clock. That is not a verdict on graphene; it is a statement about how much of the story is settled. I hold that the citation should be written around the lattice clock and what it has shown, and should not say 'precision spectroscopy' in general.
statement.case_against: The objections that remain are real. First, lineage: a committee that regards the lattice clock as the natural end of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock story will see an excellent refinement and not a new discovery. I do not agree, but it is a judgment and not a fact. Second, attribution. Lemonde's group at SYRTE, Hollberg, Gill and NIST colleagues made contributions to lattice-clock development, and Ye's early comb and stabilisation work sits partly in territory already honoured. My recollection is that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first Sr lattice clock (around 2003 to 2005) precede the JILA and SYRTE demonstrations, and that Ye's group then drove the performance to 1e-18, but I am relying on memory and have not checked the primary papers. Third, the formal redefinition of the second has not happened, so some will say the measurement result is waiting for its consequence, and others will weigh precision below discovery of a new phenomenon in nature. Finally, graphene is a broader scientific field than the clock, and a committee that values a new field above a better instrument would reasonably choose B009.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether I consider the lattice method, rather than the instrument or the comb, the right dividing line for a citation, given that single-ion clocks (Al+, Yb+, Sr+) reach comparable uncertainties.
responses.response: Yes, I think it is the right line, and I would hold it firmly. Single-ion clocks can be as accurate, and I do not claim otherwise; the lattice clock's own claim is statistical, because a million-fold more atoms gives the stability to reach the systematic floor quickly and to compare parts of a single sample. That is why the citation should say 'optical lattice clock' and the magic wavelength, which keeps Wineland's lineage and the ion clocks outside the wording without needing to rank them. I would not accept your suggestion to put the weight on the new tests alone, however, because the redshift and constants results are consequences of the lattice and not separate discoveries; I have therefore kept both in a single citation clause.

responses.point: Pearce asks me to say whether Lemonde and others have a stronger claim than he credited, and warns that building on earlier prizes is a risk for the citation even if it is not for the physics.
responses.response: My honest answer is that I think Lemonde's group has a real claim to the early lattice-clock comparisons, but it is a claim to demonstration and confirmation, not to the original idea, and I would not call it stronger than Katori's. As I recall, the magic-wavelength proposal and the first Sr lattice-clock measurements come from Katori's group, the JILA and SYRTE results followed, and Ye's group then carried the clock to the 1e-18 level and to the redshift measurements that make the case. I have not rechecked the primary dates and I would ask whoever has the literature to do so before the vote. I agree with your drafting point, and that is why the revised citation names the lattice clock and what it achieved, not frequency metrology as a whole.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, argues that the pairing mechanism is a question for after the door is open, and values the 2011 prediction followed by the 2018 discovery as the right prize structure.
responses.response: I take your point that the unsettled mechanism does not undo the discovery, and I do not want to insist that every phenomenon be understood before it is honoured. Where we still differ is on the attribution, which you yourself call your strongest reservation and which the chair has asked about again. A three-name list that omits Cao and Fatemi, who did the hands-on 2018 work, and Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, whose earlier flat-band analysis is part of the record, leaves open a challenge to the prize that I cannot judge from atomic physics. The clock has two names and a quite clear division between idea and demonstration. You have persuaded me that B009 is a worthy first alternative, and I would not oppose it if the condensed-matter members, who know the field better than I do, judge the credit defensible.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B009 and says it is the opposite of elegant theory waiting for clues: a sharp, falsifiable prediction of flat bands that nature then delivered, with many groups reproducing the phase diagram. He has not yet seen a new physical phenomenon from the clocks.
responses.response: I accept that a falsified or confirmed prediction is a particularly clean kind of discovery, and Bistritzer-MacDonald is a good example. On your point that the clocks have not yet shown new physics, I would say that this is a fair description of the constants results, which so far set limits, but not of the gravitational redshift. Resolving a fractional frequency shift across a millimetre of one atomic cloud is a measurement of how time is defined in a gravitational field, which was not available before and is a new window and not a better ruler. I would also remind the committee that Nobel Prizes have honoured instruments that opened such windows. I would not claim that this is the same as a prediction confirmed in a new material, and I accept that a reasonable member can weigh the two differently.

responses.point: Johansson argues that the many-atom statistics make the lattice clock a distinct step and not a refinement of the Wineland clock, and that a circuit-QED prize so soon after 2025 would honour one community twice.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the statistics, and I would add that it is the reason the committee should resist calling the clock 'incremental': a hundredfold gain in averaging speed is what allowed new measurements and not only smaller error bars. On circuit QED I remain at the same place, which is that the physics is strong but the timing is poor, and I note your own conflict declaration for those groups. I would still go beyond you in one respect, which is that I do not think the clock should be defended by its eventual application to timekeeping. I would keep the citation on the physics and let the redefinition of the second follow.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B009 and says the continuum-model band structure is quantitatively checked against scanning-probe and transport data, and that the three-person theory-plus-experiment structure fits the prize rules without an arbitrary cut.
responses.response: The quantitative checks you describe are the sort of theory-experiment agreement that persuades me, and they are the reason I keep B009 as my first alternative. Your own uncertainty, whether the experimental credit goes to Jarillo-Herrero alone or includes Cao, is however the one that I think the committee must settle before awarding the prize, because a three-name limit forces an arbitrary cut on the experimental side whatever one does. I would be grateful if you could say whether, in your view, the condensed-matter community would accept Jarillo-Herrero alone as the experimental name; if so, I would be easier about the trio than I am now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the magic-wavelength lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as the continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes. This is a judgment I cannot settle with a measurement.
Priority among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Hollberg and the single-ion clock community for the first lattice-clock demonstrations. I rely on memory and ask for a primary-literature check before the vote.

Whether the condensed-matter members consider the B009 attribution (Cao and Fatemi, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) defensible with three names; I cannot judge it myself, and it is the main thing that could move me.
How much weight a precision-measurement result deserves against a discovery in a new material, and whether the 1e-18 comparisons and redshift tests are 'new physics' or 'new tools'.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH Zurich attosecond groups. None of the credited names on B049, B009 or B012 is among my collaborators, and my storage-ring and attosecond work is in a neighbouring field. I also note that atomic structure theory of the type I do is used to compute clock systematic shifts such as blackbody radiation, so I am professionally close to the subject matter though not to either laureate. I have no conflict to add since round 1, and I flag this proximity for transparency and not as grounds for recusal.
